title: SIU probes death of former boxer; Taser shocks have killed 50; Peel police used stun gun on victim Clerk called 911 over disturbance: [ONT Edition]
article: The provincial Special Investigations Unit is looking into the death of a semi-pro boxer who was hit with a charge from a Taser gun during a disturbance at a motel near Pearson airport early yesterday.

Peel police said 29-year-old Jerry Knight of Brampton was dead on arrival at Peel Memorial Hospital. Witnesses said the electric gun was used to try and subdue the man who had "gone berserk" in the office of the White Knight Motel on Dixie Rd.

The SIU, which investigates whenever police operations result in the death or serious injury of a civilian, is releasing few details about the incident. An autopsy is expected to be done today at the Centre for Forensic Sciences in Toronto.
Knight, who is believed to be single, had booked into the motel around 7 30 a.m. Friday with a bag that held boxing equipment, including gloves, shorts and workout clothes.
Motel owner Mike Capo, 64, said the man was not seen again until he came into the motel office around 2 a.m. claiming he had lost his key and asking to be let into his motel room.
The desk clerk let the man into his room, 114, but a short while later the man returned to the office in a disturbed state.
"He asked for a receipt, was given one and then he immediately ate the piece of paper," Capo said.
"He then started hitting things and throwing things around and tried to get over the counter into the office area," Capo said.
"It's very sad. I haven't had anything like this happen since I got into the motel business in 1978."
Four Peel Region police officers responded to the motel clerk's 911 call. Capo said they tried to reason with the man "to get him to calm down," but their efforts apparently failed.
The officers then called in the Peel tactical unit, which used a Taser while trying to arrest the man. One Peel officer is reported to have suffered minor injuries in the scuffle.
The man was rushed to Peel Memorial Hospital by ambulance but was pronounced dead on arrival, SIU spokesperson Rose Bliss said.
"We have seven investigators on the case and one Peel officer so far has been named a subject officer in the investigation."
The man, who was a championship high school boxer in the early '90s and had fought some semi-pro matches in the intervening years, was said to be "known to police."

Since 2001 at least 50 people - most of them in the United States, but two in Canada - have died after being shocked by Tasers. The weapons, designed as non-lethal alternatives to guns, shoot twin darts that disable a suspect by discharging 50,000 volts of electricity. They are used by Toronto police's emergency task force.
Both Canadian deaths occurred last year in B.C. as police were making arrests.

Taser International, the Arizona-based company that manufactures the weapons, maintains its products are not lethal, even for people with heart conditions or pacemakers, the New York Times reports today.
The company blames the deaths on drug overdoses or other factors, and says they would have happened anyway.

But Andrew Podgorski, a Canadian electrical engineer who carried out studies on stun guns in 1989, said he was certain that Tasers are dangerous for people with pacemakers, and wants more research to determine if others are vulnerable.
John Wikswo, a Vanderbilt University biomedical engineer, said small electrical shocks can kill people whose hearts are weakened because of disease or cocaine use.
But, he added, no one knows whether the Taser's current crosses the threshold for such people.
"Their testing scheme has not included the possibility that there is a subset of the population that is exquisitely sensitive," Wikswo said. "That alone means they have not done adequate testing."

Meanwhile, police and investor support for the weapon continues to soar. Investors have bid up the company's shares 60-fold since last February, giving Taser - which was near bankruptcy in 1999 - a value of $1.2 billion (U.S.).
Taser's executives and directors have sold $60 million in shares since last November, according to public filings.
